figures.alt: The Castello Plan of New Amsterdam in 1660, redrawn in 1916, showing the fort at the tip of Manhattan, the wall across the town, canals, gardens, and ships in the harbor
figures.caption: New Amsterdam in 1660, redrawn 1916

primary_sources: Castello Plan of New Amsterdam (1660), redrawn by John Wolcott Adams and Isaac Newton Phelps Stokes (1916)

options.text: A small trading post surrounded by rivals needed defenses more than it needed farmland.

options.misconception: Reads the fort as the whole purpose — the harbor full of ships shows trade paid for the fort.
options.text: The Dutch West India Company planned New Amsterdam as a military fortress with no trade.

options.misconception: The Dutch depended on Native trading partners for furs; the wall faced European rivals.
options.text: The Dutch built the wall to keep Native peoples out of the town entirely.

options.misconception: The wall ran across Manhattan island itself, facing the land side — not along an English border.
options.text: The wall marked the boundary between Dutch and English colonies.

rationales.A: The plan shows a compact town with a fort and wall — a trading post that had to defend itself among English, French, and Spanish rivals.
rationales.B: The harbor full of ships and the canals show trade was the point; the fort protected the trade, not replaced it.
rationales.C: The Dutch depended on Native trading partners for furs; the wall was built against European rivals, not against their trading partners.
rationales.D: The wall ran across Manhattan island itself, facing the land side — not along any boundary with an English colony.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the defenses. A fort at the tip and a wall across the town — this is a place that expected trouble.
2. Ask who the trouble was. Background: New Netherland sat between English colonies to the north and south, and the Dutch fought the English and French for trade.
3. Ask what the town was for. Ships in the harbor, canals in the streets — the town moved furs and goods.
4. Put the two together. The Dutch spent money on walls because the trade was worth protecting.
Remember: defenses tell you what a place feared losing, and here it was the trade, not the land.

stimulus.text: The Castello Plan of New Amsterdam in 1660, redrawn by John Wolcott Adams and Isaac Newton Phelps Stokes in 1916 from the original plan. The map shows the town at the southern tip of Manhattan: the fort stands at the tip, a wall runs across the town, canals cut through the streets, and houses stand among gardens and orchards. Ships crowd the harbor at the left, where the Hudson meets the sea.
